**House of Representatives**

| Period | Event | Significance |
|--------|-------|--------------|
| 1845‑1880 | The House had a *select* Rules Committee in 1845 whose chair was chosen by the speaker, not by the majority party.  | The committee’s power was largely a personal tool of the Speaker, not a party‑controlled lever. |
| **December 1980 (51st Congress)** | The House reorganised its committee system and made the Rules Committee a permanent *standing* committee.  | Immediately after the Republican takeover the party that held the House automatically controlled the committee – the chair and membership reflected the majority party. |
| **1880** | The Committee was granted a permanent standing status (and began to be called the “Rules Committee”) when the Republicans took control of the House.  | In practice, since that re‑organization the party that holds the majority has effectively determined the House’s rules. |

**Senate**

| Period | Event | Significance |
|--------|-------|--------------|
| **December 7 1835** | The Senate “organized its committee system on the principle that the majority party should chair the major committees.” | This was the first time major committees—including that which would become the Rules Committee—were directly controlled by the majority party. |
| **December 9 1874** | The committee that would become the Rules Committee was established as a standing committee. | From its inception onward it was chaired by the majority party; the chair and membership reflected the majority. |
| **1947** | The committee was renamed the *Committee on Rules and Administration* and oversaw additional affairs, but it remained majority‑controlled. | The majority’s control of this committee persisted and continues to this day. |

---

**Answer to the question**

* *House of Representatives*: The majority party gained effective control of the body that determines House rules when the Rules Committee was turned into a permanent standing committee in **1880** (the 51st Congress).  
* *United States Senate*: The principle of majority control of standing committees was adopted in **1835**, and the Rules Committee specifically became a standing committee under majority control in **1874**. Thus, from 1874 onward the Senate’s rules‑setting committee has been controlled by the party holding the Senate majority.

The **Committee on Rules** (or more commonly the **Rules Committee**) is a [committee] of the [United States House of Representatives]. It is responsible for the rules under which [bills] "Bill (law)") will be presented to the House of Representatives, unlike other committees, which often deal with a specific area of policy. The committee is often considered one of the most powerful committees as it influences the introduction and process of legislation through the House. Thus it has garnered the nickname the "traffic cop of [Congress] "Congress (United States)")". A "special rule" resolution (also referred to simply as a "rule") is a simple resolution of the House of Representatives, usually reported by the Committee on Rules, to permit the immediate consideration of a legislative measure, notwithstanding the usual order of business, and to prescribe conditions for its debate and amendment.[[2]]

## Jurisdiction

[[edit]]

The ['regular' process] "Regular order (United States Congress)") to pass a bill in the house is complicated and prone to delays and obstruction by the minority. Because of this, in practice, bills (other than those that are uncontroversial) are almost always debated under a so-called 'special rule' reported by the Rules Committee. This rule usually restricts the lengths of debate and number and type of amendments allowed (if any).

### Special rules

[[edit]]

When a bill is reported out of another committee with legislative jurisdiction, it is placed on the appropriate [House Calendar] for debate. Common practice, though, is for bills reported from committees to be considered in the Rules Committee, which then passes a so-called "special rule" (a resolution allowing for consideration of a bill, establishing how long and under what rules the full body will debate the proposition). A "special rule" resolution (also known simply as a "rule") is [privileged] under the Standing Rules of the House, meaning it is immediately subject to a debate and a vote by the full House upon being reported by the Rules Committee. If a "special rule" resolution providing for consideration of a bill is passed, then such bill must be considered by the House at such a time and under such limitations as the resolution has set. In practice, a bill can get to a floor vote only if a "special rule" resolution providing for its consideration is passed (unless the Speaker grants a vote on [suspension of the rules], which requires two-thirds of votes cast in order to pass).

Consideration by the full body can occur in one of two forums: the [Committee of the Whole] "Committee of the Whole (United States House of Representatives)"), or on the floor of the full House of Representatives itself. Different traditions govern whether the Committee of the Whole or the House itself will debate a given resolution, and the Rules Committee generally sets the forum under which a proposition will be debated and the amendment/time limitations for every measure, too. The **Senate Committee on Rules and Administration**, also called the **Senate Rules and Administration Committee**, is responsible for the rules of the [United States Senate], administration of congressional buildings, and with credentials and qualifications of members of the Senate, including responsibility for contested elections. The committee is not as powerful as its House counterpart, the [House Committee on Rules], as it does not set the terms of debate for individual legislative proposals, since the Senate has a tradition of open debate. Some members of the committee are also [ex officio] members of the [Joint Committee on the Library] and the [Joint Committee on Printing].

## History

[[edit]]

Further information: [United States Senate Committee on Rules]

The Committee was first created as the [Select Committee to Revise the Rules of the Senate] on December 3, 1867. On December 9, 1874, it became a standing committee.

On January 2, 1947, its name was changed to the Committee on Rules and Administration, and it took over the functions of the following committees:

* [Committee to Audit and Control the Contingent Expenses of the Senate]

**House of Representatives**

| Period | Event | Significance |
|--------|-------|--------------|
| 1845‑1880 | The House had a *select* Rules Committee in 1845 whose chair was chosen by the speaker, not by the majority party.  | The committee’s power was largely a personal tool of the Speaker, not a party‑controlled lever. |
| **December 1980 (51st Congress)** | The House reorganised its committee system and made the Rules Committee a permanent *standing* committee.  | Immediately after the Republican takeover the party that held the House automatically controlled the committee – the chair and membership reflected the majority party. |
| **1880** | The Committee was granted a permanent standing status (and began to be called the “Rules Committee”) when the Republicans took control of the House.  | In practice, since that re‑organization the party that holds the majority has effectively determined the House’s rules. |

**Senate**

| Period | Event | Significance |
|--------|-------|--------------|
| **December 7 1835** | The Senate “organized its committee system on the principle that the majority party should chair the major committees.” | This was the first time major committees—including that which would become the Rules Committee—were directly controlled by the majority party. |
| **December 9 1874** | The committee that would become the Rules Committee was established as a standing committee. | From its inception onward it was chaired by the majority party; the chair and membership reflected the majority. |
| **1947** | The committee was renamed the *Committee on Rules and Administration* and oversaw additional affairs, but it remained majority‑controlled. | The majority’s control of this committee persisted and continues to this day. |

---

**Answer to the question**

* *House of Representatives*: The majority party gained effective control of the body that determines House rules when the Rules Committee was turned into a permanent standing committee in **1880** (the 51st Congress).  
* *United States Senate*: The principle of majority control of standing committees was adopted in **1835**, and the Rules Committee specifically became a standing committee under majority control in **1874**. Thus, from 1874 onward the Senate’s rules‑setting committee has been controlled by the party holding the Senate majority.
